readerTitle: Two firms, one flood: why one was back in two days
caseNote: 가상 사례 (병원 청소 용역 업체 두 곳, 회사 안의 급여팀) + 실제 연구 (Simchi-Levi 외, 회복 시간·생존 시간) + 실제 기업 (2000년 Philips 공장 화재와 Nokia·Ericsson)
insight: 회복력은 사고를 피하는 능력이 아니다. 의존하는 것마다 '버틸 수 있는 시간'과 '되살리는 데 걸리는 시간'을 비교하고, 그 차이가 가장 큰 곳부터 메우는 일이다.
misconception: 회복력은 재고를 넉넉히 쌓아 두는 것이다. 지출이 큰 공급처일수록 위험도 크다.

sources.text: Simchi-Levi, D., Schmidt, W., & Wei, Y. (2014). From Superstorms to Factory Fires: Managing Unpredictable Supply-Chain Disruptions. Harvard Business Review.
Sheffi, Y. (2005). The Resilient Enterprise. MIT Press. (2000년 Philips 앨버커키 공장 화재와 Nokia·Ericsson의 대응)
청소 업체와 급여팀 사례의 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 'time to recover'와 'time to survive' 개념은 Simchi-Levi 외(HBR 2014)와 관련 후속 연구(Ford 사례)에 나옵니다. 두 용어가 처음 등장한 문헌을 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요.

Philips 공장 화재(2000년 3월, 미국 뉴멕시코 앨버커키): Nokia는 이상을 빨리 감지해 대체 공급을 확보했고, Ericsson은 단일 공급처에 의존해 큰 매출 손실을 입었다는 내용은 Sheffi(2005) 등 여러 자료에 나옵니다. 손실 금액은 자료마다 달라 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다. Ericsson이 이후 휴대폰 사업을 Sony와의 합작사로 넘긴 것(2001)은 화재 하나만의 결과가 아니므로 '여러 원인 중 하나'로만 표현했습니다.
가상 수치 계산: Brightline은 재고 5일, 대체품 승인 약 4주(28일) → 공백 약 23일. Northway는 재고 5일, 전환 2일 → 공백 없음(3일 여유).
'위험이 가장 큰 품목이 지출이 큰 품목과 일치하지 않는 경우가 많다'는 문장은 Simchi-Levi 외의 Ford 분석에서 나온 관찰로 알려져 있습니다. 카드에는 수치 없이 일반 원칙으로만 적었습니다.

cards.title: Two firms, one flood: why one was back in two days
body: Two cleaning contractors serve hospitals in the same city. Same size, same prices, same supplier for their disinfectant.
One night the supplier's warehouse floods. One firm is back to normal in two days. The other spends three weeks apologizing to clients. Neither saw the flood coming.

image.label: Two cleaning vans, one moving, one stuck
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 비 오는 거리에 똑같은 청소 업체 밴 두 대. 한 대는 병원으로 출발하고, 다른 한 대는 텅 빈 선반 앞에 멈춰 있음. 배경에 물에 잠긴 창고. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You run one of the two firms.
body: Hospitals only allow disinfectants they have approved. You have a budget for one change to protect your business from supply shocks. Which do you pick?

options.text: Triple your stock of every supply you use
options.feedback: You buy time on everything, but you tie up cash and shelf space in items you could replace in an hour. And three times the stock still runs out eventually.

options.text: Find the supplies that would take longest to replace, and get a backup approved for those
options.feedback: You spend little on the easy items and protect the one that could stop you for weeks. The next card shows why that matters.

options.text: Negotiate a lower price with your single supplier and buy insurance
options.feedback: Insurance may pay for some losses, but it doesn't clean a single hospital room. Clients care that the work gets done.

cards.title: The difference was a gap, not luck.
body: Both firms had five days of disinfectant on hand. **Northway** had already gotten a second product approved by its hospitals. **Brightline** had not, and a new approval took about four weeks.

cards.title: Resilience
body: **Resilience** is a business's ability to keep serving customers through a disruption and recover quickly.

Researchers David Simchi-Levi and colleagues suggest two numbers for each thing you depend on. *Time to survive*: how long you can keep going without it. *Time to recover*: how long until it is back or replaced.
When time to recover is longer than time to survive, you have a gap. That gap is your real risk.

image.label: Two bars: time to survive vs time to recover
image.brief: 가로 막대 두 개 비교 인포그래픽. 위쪽 "Time to survive 5 days", 아래쪽 "Time to recover 28 days". 두 막대 끝 사이의 빈 구간을 붉은색으로 칠하고 "The gap" 라벨.

cards.softwareNote: For a software company, a dependency might be one cloud region, one payment provider or one engineer who knows the billing code. Ask the same two questions about each.

cards.title: A factory fire, two phone makers.
body: In 2000, a fire hit a Philips chip plant in New Mexico. Nokia and Ericsson both bought parts from it.
Nokia spotted the delays early, pushed for answers and quickly lined up other sources. Ericsson depended on that plant with no ready backup, and lost months of phone sales.
Yossi Sheffi's book *The Resilient Enterprise* tells the story. It is often cited as one of several reasons Ericsson later moved its phone business into a joint venture with Sony.

cards.title: You can't back up everything.
body: Backups cost money: second suppliers, extra approvals, spare stock, people trained twice. Do it for everything and you lose the efficiency that keeps prices low.
So rank by gap, not by spend. The riskiest item is often a cheap, boring one, like an approved disinfectant, that nobody watches.
And backups decay. An approved supplier you never order from may not be ready when you call. Use or test it now and then.

cards.title: Now it's a payroll team inside a big company.
body: Your team pays 2,000 employees every month. Only one specialist, Dana, knows how to fix the payroll file when the bank rejects it. That happens a few times a year. Payroll must go out within two days.

options.feedback: It closes the gap, but at a full salary for a task that happens a few times a year. A cheaper fix may do the same job.

options.text: Have Dana write the steps down, train a colleague, and let the colleague handle the next rejection
options.feedback: Time to recover drops from weeks to hours, for a few days of work. Letting the colleague do a real fix keeps the backup from going stale.

options.text: Leave it. Dana has never missed a payday
options.feedback: That's a record of luck, not a plan. If Dana is away during a rejection, 2,000 people get paid late.

cards.title: Resilience is measured in days.
body: For anything you depend on, compare how long you can last without it with how long it takes to recover. Fix the biggest gaps first.
**Try it today:** list five things your business can't run without. Next to each, write two numbers: days you could survive, days to recover. Circle the biggest gap.
